name: Gas
seoDesc: Gas: work out fuel price from the fuel economy and the fuel used. A free everyday life calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Gas calculator the fuel economy, the fuel used and the cost of the trip and it returns fuel price. It is built for a practical question that turns up in daily life. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Gas calculator work?
sections.html:
The Gas calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports fuel price in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the car and the trip type); then you type in the fuel economy (Plan a trip and fuel costs), the fuel used (Plan a trip and fuel costs), the cost of the trip (Plan a trip and fuel costs) and the cost of the trip (Plan a trip and fuel costs).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Gas calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Fuel price=cost of the trip ÷ fuel used
Cost per person=cost of the trip ÷ number of people
Distance=fuel used × fuel economy
Fuel used=cost of the trip ÷ (fuel price)
Fuel economy=distance ÷ fuel used

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Fuel economy, opening in liters per 100 kilometers
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Volume, opening in liters
  • Volume, opening in liters
  • Volume, opening in liters
  • Volume, opening in liters
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Gas calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the fuel economy, the fuel used and the cost of the trip — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Gas calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns fuel price, derived from the fuel economy, the fuel used and the cost of the trip. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Gas calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the fuel economy, the fuel used and the cost of the trip, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter fuel economy (Plan a trip and fuel costs) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Fuel economy (Plan a trip and fuel costs) opens in liters per 100 kilometers and the chip beside it offers 10 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Gas calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
